papers.title: InsightRAG: Aggregating Distributed Scholarly Judgments for Scientific Survey Generation
papers.abstract: The rapid growth of scientific literature makes survey writing increasingly challenging, motivating automatic survey generation. Yet, existing systems must search an open space of papers and an open space of concepts with no trace of how the community itself has navigated them, leading to incomplete scope, weak taxonomies, and unreliable citations. Our core insight is that author-written Related Work sections contain the human judgments needed to address both limitations: authors curate the citations relevant to their contributions and explain how the cited works relate, yielding paths for scope reconstruction and relational evidence for organization. We propose InsightRAG. Its insight-guided retrieval follows author-supported citation relations to reconstruct a verified research scope and structure the resulting relational evidence. It aggregates these judgments under a minimum-conflict objective into a taxonomy that reflects recurring author-written perspectives in the retrieved literature, guides generation, and bounds each section's evidence. Results on ten topics show gains in scope reconstruction, taxonomy quality, citation support, and reference reliability.

papers.title: Are explicit novelty claims in research abstracts associated with higher ChatGPT scores?
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) such as ChatGPT can estimate research quality from article titles and abstracts, and decision makers may increasingly use LLM scores to support research assessment. In this context, it is a concern that LLM scores may be influenced by linguistic signals rather than the quality of the research described. This study investigates whether explicit novelty claims in research abstracts are associated with higher ChatGPT scores. Using 99,245 journal articles submitted to the UK Research Excellence Framework (REF) 2021, ChatGPT scores and percentile rank gains relative to REF departmental average scores (as a proxy for article-level scores) were compared between abstracts with and without any of 282 three-word phrases identified as indicating a novelty claim. Abstracts containing novelty claim phrases had higher mean ChatGPT quality scores in all four main REF research groupings (panels). Moreover, the score difference was higher for the originality dimension of research quality than for significance and rigour in 30 of the 34 broadly field-based Units of Assessment (UoAs) used to categorise research in the REF. Thus, explicit novelty claims probably associate with higher quality scores primarily because they associate with higher scores for the originality dimension. Follow-up tests suggested that abstracts containing novelty claims tended to rank more favourably under ChatGPT than under the REF departmental quality proxy. Whilst the findings suggest that ChatGPT may be influenced by explicit novelty claims, they do not conclusively show that novelty phrases caused the higher scores because the scores and phrases may at least partially reflect more novel research.

papers.title: Large Teams Consistently Develop Science
papers.abstract: Scientific progress depends on both developing established knowledge and disrupting it to make way for new ideas. Using the disruption index (D), our previous work showed that large teams tend to develop science, while small teams are more likely to disrupt it. Recent work challenges this finding, arguing that D mechanically depends on reference-list length. Using an alternative measure (oneD), it reaches the opposite conclusion: large teams are more disruptive. Combining Nobel Prize case studies, mathematical analysis, and large-scale publication data, we show that oneD misclassifies developmental contributions as disruptive and introduces the very sensitivity to reference-list length that it seeks to eliminate. The original measure, D, however, shows no evidence of the claimed systematic dependence on reference-list length. More fundamentally, even after controlling for reference-list length, larger teams remain more likely to produce strongly developmental work. Our findings reaffirm that large teams consistently develop science and offer new insights into the measurement of scientific disruption.

papers.title: The Geometric Function Atlas: Using What We Know About Radius Problems to Solve New Ones
papers.abstract: Usually, radius problems between Ma--Minda classes are solved one pair at a time, by fitting a disk inside the target region, providing a sufficient but not always the sharp radius. The same class appearing under different names makes comparison of results harder, with mistakes and duplication eluding detection. The Geometric Function Atlas catalogs radius problems using exact generators and a direction (source $\to$ target), ensuring unique identification. For each problem, we then compute the radius numerically, together with the point where the image first meets the target boundary. This helps us identify the sharp estimate which guides the proof we write. With this system, we were able to refine two earlier stated estimates, the disk radius for the sine $\to$ modified sigmoid and sine $\to$ rational cases from $\operatorname{arsinh} c$ to $\arcsin c$, and correct earlier stated values for the crescent and exponential classes: the sharp radius is $\sin 1$ from crescent to exponential, and $\log(1+\sqrt2)$ from exponential to crescent. All four proofs follow a common strategy: an estimate that is exact at the contact point, followed by the standard extremal function. Applying the method, we derive fifteen further sharp radii, four of them known.
